screens.title: Reservation Station Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A reservation station is the scheduling unit that holds an instruction until it can execute. Each entry contains an operation code, tags (Qj and Qk) that name producers when operands are not yet available, value fields (Vj and Vk) that hold ready operands, an address offset field A for loads and stores, and a Busy flag indicating occupation. The key idea is that tags and values carry complementary information: if Qi[register] is zero at issue, the register's value copies into Vj or Vk and the corresponding Q is set to zero. If Qi is nonzero, the station records the producing reservation station's tag in Qj or Qk and leaves V invalid. This lets the station wait on a named producer rather than stalling the entire pipeline. A concrete example: an ADD that needs operands from two earlier instructions will have Qj=RS4 and Qk=0 if the first operand is pending in RS4 while the second is available. A common misconception is to think Vj/Vk will always be filled later; in fact they remain invalid until the matching tag broadcasts on the CDB and the station captures the value. Remember: reservation stations implement dynamic scheduling by linking consumers to producers through tags, not by copying results speculatively.

keyIdea.title: Reservation stations link producers to consumers
keyIdea.text: Qj/Qk hold producer tags when operands are pending; Vj/Vk hold values only when ready.

content.html:
Definition

Reservation Station Fields

Each entry stores operation, tags, values, an address offset, and a busy flag to manage readiness and allocation.

Op
Operation type (ADD, MUL, LOAD, etc.).
Qj / Qk
Tags naming reservation stations that will produce operands, or 0 if ready.
Vj / Vk
Operand values valid only when the corresponding Q is 0.
A
Address offset for memory operations.
Illustration
Example Entry (RS1)
Op: SUB
Qj: RS4
Vj: —
Qk: 0
Vk: 4
A: —
Busy: true
Concrete scenario
At issue, the station recorded RS4 as the producer for the first operand. It will wait for RS4 to broadcast and then capture Vj.
Key Takeaway

Tags, not speculative values, coordinate readiness. V fields are only valid when their Q is zero.

screens.title: Register File Structure
screens.narratorSegment: The register file in Tomasulo's design stores two pieces of information per register: a Qi tag and a Value. Qi points to the reservation station that will produce a future value; Value holds the current numeric value only when Qi equals zero. This mapping provides dynamic destination renaming without physical register file renaming: when an instruction issues to a destination register, it writes its reservation station tag into Qi, meaning subsequent instructions will record that tag rather than the old value. That behavior handles write-after-write hazards by making the newest issue determine the register mapping; older producers still broadcast, but their results do not become the register's visible value because Qi has been overwritten. A common misconception is to assume Qi prevents the old instruction from writing — it doesn't. The old instruction still broadcasts on the CDB, and any stations waiting for its tag will capture the value. However, because Qi was overwritten, the register file will only accept the value when its Qi matches the broadcaster's tag. This mechanism both enables out-of-order completion and keeps register visibility consistent.

keyIdea.title: Qi is a destination map
keyIdea.text: Qi tells consumers which reservation station will supply a register's next value; Value is valid only when Qi = 0.

content.html:
Definition

Register file: Qi and Value

Every architectural register tracks which reservation station will produce its next value through Qi. If Qi is zero, the Value field is current and available to issue logic.

Qi
Tag of the pending producer reservation station, or 0 if the register is valid.
Value
Current register value; valid only when Qi = 0.
Example
Initial state
R1=5 (Qi=0), R2=3 (Qi=0), R6 pending from RS4 → Qi[R6]=RS4
Issue example
When MUL issues to produce R6, the simulator sets Qi[R6]=RS4. Other instructions that read R6 record Qj=RS4 until RS4 broadcasts.
Common misconception

Overwriting Qi discards earlier mappings for new readers, but it does not cancel the old instruction's broadcast — the old result can still satisfy stations that were waiting for it.

screens.title: Issue Stage (Dispatch)
screens.narratorSegment: The issue stage is where an instruction first interacts with reservation stations and the register file. At issue, the unit waits for an available reservation station of the correct type. It reads the register file for each source operand: if Qi[register] is zero, the value is available and is copied into Vj or Vk while the corresponding Q field is set to zero. If Qi[register] is nonzero, the reservation station records Qj or Qk as that tag; the V field remains invalid until a broadcast. For the destination register, the issue step writes Qi[destination] = tag of the allocated reservation station. Finally, the reservation station Busy flag is set. This sequence ensures that subsequent instructions will either read values directly or record tags for producers. A concrete example from the sequence: when MUL R6, R2, R4 issues into RS4, R6's Qi is set to RS4 and any later instruction that needs R6 will set its Q to RS4 until RS4 broadcasts. A common mistake is to assume issue waits for operands to be ready; it doesn't — it records readiness via tags and allows other independent instructions to proceed. The key check: issue allocates and records mappings, not execution results.

keyIdea.title: Issue records mappings
keyIdea.text: Issue assigns reservation tags and copies values when valid; it does not wait for operand production if tags can be recorded.

content.html:
Process Flow

Issue (Dispatch)

1. Find station
Wait until an appropriate reservation station is free.
2. Read registers
If Qi=0 copy value into V; otherwise copy Qi into Q field.
3. Set destination Qi
Write the reservation station tag into the destination register's Qi.
4. Mark busy
Reservation station Busy becomes true; instruction awaits operands or execution unit.
Example
MUL R6, R2, R4 → RS4
At issue: Qi[R6]=RS4. For sources R2 and R4, if their Qi were 0 their values copy into Vj/Vk; otherwise RS4 records Qj/Qk tags.
Pitfall

Issue does not wait for operands to arrive; it records tag links so execution can start as soon as operands broadcast.

screens.title: Execute Stage
screens.narratorSegment: Execution begins when both Qj and Qk are zero, meaning the station either had values at issue or captured them from broadcasts. For arithmetic operations, the station waits until operands are present, then the associated functional unit performs the computation. For memory operations, the station computes an effective address (base plus offset A) and interacts with the memory unit before completing. Latency matters: each functional unit takes a fixed number of cycles to complete its operation in the model, so execution spans multiple cycles for some operations. An important concrete point is that issuing does not guarantee immediate execution; a station may be ready but stall if the functional unit is busy. Misunderstandings often mix station readiness with unit availability — both must be true for execution to start. In the sample sequence, MUL in RS4 started executing early because its operands were ready, while DIV waited for the result of an ADD that was itself dependent. Keep in mind: execute consumes cycles proportional to unit latency and produces a result that will later be broadcast, so overlapping execution of independent ready stations is how Tomasulo gains parallelism.

keyIdea.title: Execution requires readiness and unit availability
keyIdea.text: A station executes only when Qj and Qk are zero and a functional unit is free; latencies determine overlap potential.

content.html:
Execute

When execution begins

Execution requires both operands ready (Qj = Qk = 0) and access to a functional unit. Memory operations add address calculation and memory unit timing.

Operand readiness
Stations capture values from CDB broadcasts; only then can execution start.
Unit allocation
A ready station still waits if the functional unit is occupied.
Latency
Different operations have different cycle costs that determine overlap possibilities.
Scenario
MUL (3-cycle) starts early
If both operands are ready at issue, MUL occupies the multiplier and completes after its latency, broadcasting its result.
Misconception

Ready stations always execute immediately — not true. Functional units can be the bottleneck even when operands are present.

screens.title: Write Result Stage and the Common Data Bus (CDB)
screens.narratorSegment: When a functional unit completes, it broadcasts the result and its producing reservation station tag on the Common Data Bus. Every reservation station watches the CDB: if a station has Qj or Qk equal to that tag, it records the result into Vj or Vk and clears the matching Q to zero. The register file also listens: if Qi for any register equals the broadcaster's tag, the register updates its Value field and sets Qi to zero. After broadcasting, the producing reservation station is marked not busy. The CDB is a single broadcast channel in the classic design, which means only one result can be sent per cycle; if two units finish in the same cycle, one must wait, creating a structural hazard. Designers mitigate this by adding additional result buses or pipelining writes, trading area for fewer write conflicts. A common misunderstanding is thinking the register file receives results directly from functional units; instead, tag matching at write time determines whether the register accepts a broadcast. The CDB thus implements dynamic forwarding and resolves operand dependencies at write time rather than at commit time.

keyIdea.title: CDB: single broadcast, multiple listeners
keyIdea.text: Broadcasts match tags: stations capture values, registers clear Qi when their tag is seen, and the producer frees its station.

content.html:
Architecture

Write Result & CDB

Complete operations broadcast a (tag, value) pair on the CDB. Reservation stations and the register file capture values by matching tags.

Broadcast
A tag and its result are sent on the CDB once the unit finishes.
Capture
Stations with matching Q fields capture the value and clear their Q.
Register update
If Qi[reg] matches the tag, Value updates and Qi becomes zero.
Trade-offs
Single bus hazard
Only one station can broadcast per cycle; simultaneous completions create a structural conflict.
Mitigation
Designers add more result buses or pipeline writes to reduce conflicts, trading area and power for throughput.
Key Takeaway

CDB semantics determine when stations and registers observe values; bus width affects structural conflicts and performance.

screens.title: Example Walkthrough — Instruction Sequence
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through the provided instruction sequence and follow tags and broadcasts across cycles. Begin with registers R1.. R5 valid and all Qi = 0. Cycle 1 issues MUL R6, R2, R4 into RS4 and sets Qi[R6] = RS4. Cycle 2 issues SUB R8, R6, R5 into RS1; because R6 is pending, RS1 records Qj = RS4 while Qk = 0 and sets Qi[R8] = RS1. Also in cycle 2 MUL can start executing because its operands were available. Cycle 3 issues ADD R10, R8, R6 into RS2; RS2 records Qj = RS1 and Qk = RS4 and sets Qi[R10] = RS2. Assume MUL has 3-cycle latency: it completes in cycle 3 and broadcasts its result (6) on the CDB. RS1 captures R6 = 6 and clears Qj. RS2 captures the R6 value for its Qk. Cycle 4 issues DIV into RS5 and ADD into RS3. SUB then begins execution because its operands are ready; when SUB completes in cycle 5 it broadcasts, allowing RS2 to see R8 and start execution. Continue this trace to observe when Qi values return to zero and when registers become valid. The cycle-by-cycle mapping shows where parallelism helped and where dependencies serialized the flow.

keyIdea.title: Trace shows tag flow
keyIdea.text: Cycle-level tracing reveals when tags are set, when broadcasts clear Q fields, and how execution overlaps.

content.html:
Timeline

Cycle-by-cycle walkthrough

Cycle 1
Issue MUL → RS4; Qi[R6]=RS4.
Cycle 2
Issue SUB → RS1; RS1 Qj=RS4 (R6 pending). MUL starts execute.
Cycle 3
Issue ADD → RS2; MUL completes and broadcasts value 6 on CDB. RS1 and RS2 capture R6.
Cycle 4
Issue DIV and ADD; SUB begins execution with captured operands.
Cycle 5
SUB completes and broadcasts. RS2 and RS3 capture R8 and R6 values, starting their execution soon after.
Cycle 6–14
ADDs and DIV proceed; DIV occupies many cycles and eventually broadcasts. Total observed cycles: 14 under assumed latencies.
Key Takeaway

Tracing shows when tags are written and when broadcasts free waiting stations; this is how out-of-order execution becomes visible.

screens.title: Cycle Analysis and Latency Effects
screens.narratorSegment: Latency values for functional units change how much work can overlap. In the example we assumed a 3-cycle multiplier, 1-cycle add/sub, and a 6-cycle divider. Those numbers determine which operations can complete and broadcast early, unlocking dependent instructions. A key observation from the walkthrough: the MUL completed quickly and seeded other operations, while the DIV's long latency stretched the tail of execution. However, note the insightful point in the source: even though Tomasulo enables out-of-order execution, a long dependency chain can remove the advantage because each instruction waits for a predecessor's result. In our sequence the dependency chain involving R6→R8→R10→R12 limited parallelism; independent instructions like SUB R6,R2,R3 or ADD F8 in the hands-on example can run in parallel with the chain. If multiple reservation stations were available for the same unit type, more independent instructions could be in-flight, but added stations only help when there are independent instructions to feed them. Also remember the CDB's single-bus limitation: if two units complete in the same cycle, one must delay its broadcast. The overall lesson: latency, station count, and bus bandwidth together determine real speedup.

keyIdea.text: Fast units free results sooner to unblock dependents; long latencies or single-bus writes can limit out-of-order gains.

content.html:
Latency Analysis

How latencies affect execution

Assumed latencies
MUL: 3 cycles · ADD/SUB: 1 cycle · DIV: 6 cycles
Fast completions produce early broadcasts that let dependents start sooner.
Dependency chain
A chain of dependent instructions serializes progress regardless of out-of-order features.
Independent instructions benefit most from extra stations or units.
Station count
More stations allow more in-flight independent instructions if there are enough functional units.
CDB bandwidth
Single-bus writes can serialize results even when units finish in parallel.
Design trade-off
Adding buses or units reduces stalls but costs area and power.

screens.title: Out-of-Order vs In-Order on the Example
screens.narratorSegment: Compare the example's timeline under Tomasulo-style out-of-order execution with an in-order baseline. In-order execution would force each instruction to complete before the next begins, so with latencies of 3,1,1,6,1 the total cycles add roughly in sequence, producing a sum that represents purely sequential completion. Tomasulo attempts to overlap independent operations: while a long-latency DIV is in progress, later independent instructions can execute and complete, reducing idle cycles. However, the chapter's walkthrough explicitly shows a case where out-of-order execution did not yield a lower cycle count because dependencies formed a chain: results needed by later operations forced serialization. This contrast highlights a misconception: out-of-order execution is not a silver bullet. It requires independent instructions and sufficient resources. Use a concrete comparison: if independent instructions like an extra SUB or ADD exist, Tomasulo's mechanism will overlap execution and reduce total cycles. Without those independent instructions, additional reservation stations or buses won't improve the serialized chain. The practical point for designers and programmers is to expose independent work and avoid long producer-consumer chains when possible. screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Simulator Design
screens.narratorSegment: The recommended hands-on activity is to implement a cycle-level Tomasulo simulator that accepts instruction sequences and prints reservation station contents, register Qi values, and CDB broadcasts per cycle. Start by modeling reservation stations as a list of entries with fields Op, Qj, Qk, Vj, Vk, A, Busy. Model the register file with Qi and Value fields for each register. Implement an issue routine that finds a free station, reads Qi to decide whether to copy a value or a tag, sets Qi[destination], and marks the station busy. Implement execute logic that checks stations whose Q fields are zero and decrements remaining latency when a unit is occupied. When a unit completes, schedule a CDB broadcast that in the same cycle writes to waiting stations and to registers whose Qi matches the tag. Be careful implementing CDB arbitration: only one broadcast per cycle unless you explicitly support multiple buses. A concrete exercise: simulate the provided sample sequence and log per-cycle snapshots. Then change the number of reservation stations and count total cycles to produce a plot of cycles versus station count. This exercise forces you to confront tag management, write conflicts, and the visible effects of latency and resource counts.

screens.title: WAW Hazards, Qi Overwrites, and Visibility
screens.narratorSegment: Write-after-write hazards in Tomasulo's model are handled by the register file's Qi mapping rather than by cancelling older instructions. When a new instruction issues to a destination register that already has Qi ≠ 0, the simulator overwrites Qi with the new station's tag. This means subsequent instructions will reference the newer tag and no longer wait for the older producer. The older instruction still executes and broadcasts its result on the CDB; any reservation stations that recorded the older tag as a source will capture that value when it broadcasts. The register file, however, will update its Value only if its Qi equals the broadcasting tag at the time of broadcast. So the old result can be invisible to the architectural register if Qi has been overwritten. This behavior implements a form of dynamic renaming: the newest producer becomes the register's mapped supplier. A common misconception is to think overwriting Qi aborts the old producer; it does not. This distinction matters when reasoning about correctness and visibility: broadcasts always reach listening stations, but registers accept a broadcast only when the tag matches their current Qi. Consider this when designing commit logic or when interpreting simulator logs.

keyIdea.text: Overwriting Qi hands future readers to the newest producer; old broadcasts still can satisfy earlier-dependent stations but not the register if Qi changed.

content.html:
Process

WAW and Qi overwrites

When a new instruction claims a destination, Qi is overwritten to the new tag. The older producer still broadcasts, but the register only updates if Qi matches that older tag.

Implication
This prevents younger instructions from observing older writes as the register's future value, implementing write-order semantics via renaming.
Concrete example
Scenario
If RS_old will write R1 but before it does a newer RS_new issues to R1, Qi[R1] points to RS_new. When RS_old later broadcasts, Qi[R1] != RS_old so the register won't accept that older value.

screens.title: Assessment Idea and Practical Questions
screens.narratorSegment: A solid assessment asks students to explain structural behaviors and to reason about resource trade-offs. Example question: "Why does the register file need a Qi for each register, and what happens when a new instruction issues to a register whose Qi is already nonzero?" The expected answer is that Qi maps the register to a producing reservation station; issuing overwrites Qi so the newest producer becomes the register's mapped future writer, and older writes remain broadcast-capable but no longer update the register if Qi changed. Another important assessment: "What occurs if two reservation stations complete in the same cycle and both want to broadcast on the CDB?" The correct explanation highlights a structural hazard: only one broadcast per cycle on a single CDB, so one write must be delayed; designers can add more buses or pipeline writes to mitigate this. For a practical task, ask students to vary reservation station counts in their simulator and plot total cycles vs number of stations. The change in slope reveals whether the workload has independent instructions to benefit from parallelism or is bottlenecked by dependency chains or the CDB.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these quick reference points handy when you build or debug a Tomasulo simulator. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Quick Reference

Quick Reference

Issue rule
If Qi=0 copy Value to V; else copy Qi into Q.
Broadcast rule
One broadcast per cycle per CDB; listeners match tags to capture values.

New issues overwrite Qi; registers update only when Qi equals the broadcast tag.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will revisit Tomasulo's algorithm with a focus on concrete structures and the cycle-by-cycle behavior that drives out-of-order execution. We'll make the reservation station concrete: its fields, how the register file uses Qi to point to pending results, and how the Common Data Bus forwards completed values so dependent instructions can proceed. You will see a short instruction sequence and follow how tags propagate, how results broadcast, and why long dependency chains limit parallelism. We'll also walk through common hazards such as write-after-write mapping and the single-bus limitation, and then connect these ideas to a small simulator activity you can implement to experiment with different counts of reservation stations and buses. By the end you'll be able to explain why Tomasulo's design renames destinations, how reservation entries capture values or tags at issue, and when the CDB becomes a bottleneck. Think of this lesson as a careful map: the structures and the rules, a concrete example, and a set of practices you can test in a simulator. What will be the bottleneck in your case: units, stations, or the CDB?

These learning objectives will guide your work through the chapter. First, you will implement Tomasulo's algorithm in a simulator that models issue, execute, and write stages; that practice forces you to handle tags, reservation entries, and the CDB explicitly. Second, you will be able to explain the reservation station structure: what each field means and how Qj/Qk versus Vj/Vk determine readiness. Third, you will describe the Common Data Bus and its role in delivering results to waiting stations and to the register file. Fourth, you will analyze performance on a sample instruction sequence to see when out-of-order execution gives speedups and when dependency chains limit them. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: implementation, structural understanding, communication of broadcast behavior, and cycle-level performance analysis. These skills matter because building or reading a simulator reveals subtle hazards, like write conflicts on the CDB or destination renaming effects on the register file. The smallest experiments — varying reservation station counts or observing simultaneous completions — make these ideas concrete.

This second objectives slide explains why each skill matters when you diagnose performance or design hardware. Implementing Tomasulo in a simulator forces you to make decisions about tags, latency, and the single-bus constraint; that hands-on work reveals structural hazards that are otherwise abstract. Understanding reservation stations is key because those fields determine when an instruction can start execution; Qj/Qk carry pending producers while Vj/Vk hold ready operands. Describing the Common Data Bus is essential because it is the mechanism that resolves dependencies at runtime — if the bus is single and two units finish together, one will delay. Analyzing performance ties the prior skills together: by running a sample sequence you see when independent instructions overlap and when a dependency chain serializes work. These skills let you answer design questions such as whether to add reservation stations, duplicate result buses, or change functional unit latencies. Each choice trades area and complexity for reduced stalls, and your simulator experiments make that trade-off visible.

A reservation station is the scheduling unit that holds an instruction until it can execute. Each entry contains an operation code, tags (Qj and Qk) that name producers when operands are not yet available, value fields (Vj and Vk) that hold ready operands, an address offset field A for loads and stores, and a Busy flag indicating occupation. The key idea is that tags and values carry complementary information: if Qi[register] is zero at issue, the register's value copies into Vj or Vk and the corresponding Q is set to zero. If Qi is nonzero, the station records the producing reservation station's tag in Qj or Qk and leaves V invalid. This lets the station wait on a named producer rather than stalling the entire pipeline. A concrete example: an ADD that needs operands from two earlier instructions will have Qj=RS4 and Qk=0 if the first operand is pending in RS4 while the second is available. A common misconception is to think Vj/Vk will always be filled later; in fact they remain invalid until the matching tag broadcasts on the CDB and the station captures the value. Remember: reservation stations implement dynamic scheduling by linking consumers to producers through tags, not by copying results speculatively.

The register file in Tomasulo's design stores two pieces of information per register: a Qi tag and a Value. Qi points to the reservation station that will produce a future value; Value holds the current numeric value only when Qi equals zero. This mapping provides dynamic destination renaming without physical register file renaming: when an instruction issues to a destination register, it writes its reservation station tag into Qi, meaning subsequent instructions will record that tag rather than the old value. That behavior handles write-after-write hazards by making the newest issue determine the register mapping; older producers still broadcast, but their results do not become the register's visible value because Qi has been overwritten. A common misconception is to assume Qi prevents the old instruction from writing — it doesn't. The old instruction still broadcasts on the CDB, and any stations waiting for its tag will capture the value. However, because Qi was overwritten, the register file will only accept the value when its Qi matches the broadcaster's tag. This mechanism both enables out-of-order completion and keeps register visibility consistent.

The issue stage is where an instruction first interacts with reservation stations and the register file. At issue, the unit waits for an available reservation station of the correct type. It reads the register file for each source operand: if Qi[register] is zero, the value is available and is copied into Vj or Vk while the corresponding Q field is set to zero. If Qi[register] is nonzero, the reservation station records Qj or Qk as that tag; the V field remains invalid until a broadcast. For the destination register, the issue step writes Qi[destination] = tag of the allocated reservation station. Finally, the reservation station Busy flag is set. This sequence ensures that subsequent instructions will either read values directly or record tags for producers. A concrete example from the sequence: when MUL R6, R2, R4 issues into RS4, R6's Qi is set to RS4 and any later instruction that needs R6 will set its Q to RS4 until RS4 broadcasts. A common mistake is to assume issue waits for operands to be ready; it doesn't — it records readiness via tags and allows other independent instructions to proceed. The key check: issue allocates and records mappings, not execution results.

Execution begins when both Qj and Qk are zero, meaning the station either had values at issue or captured them from broadcasts. For arithmetic operations, the station waits until operands are present, then the associated functional unit performs the computation. For memory operations, the station computes an effective address (base plus offset A) and interacts with the memory unit before completing. Latency matters: each functional unit takes a fixed number of cycles to complete its operation in the model, so execution spans multiple cycles for some operations. An important concrete point is that issuing does not guarantee immediate execution; a station may be ready but stall if the functional unit is busy. Misunderstandings often mix station readiness with unit availability — both must be true for execution to start. In the sample sequence, MUL in RS4 started executing early because its operands were ready, while DIV waited for the result of an ADD that was itself dependent. Keep in mind: execute consumes cycles proportional to unit latency and produces a result that will later be broadcast, so overlapping execution of independent ready stations is how Tomasulo gains parallelism.

When a functional unit completes, it broadcasts the result and its producing reservation station tag on the Common Data Bus. Every reservation station watches the CDB: if a station has Qj or Qk equal to that tag, it records the result into Vj or Vk and clears the matching Q to zero. The register file also listens: if Qi for any register equals the broadcaster's tag, the register updates its Value field and sets Qi to zero. After broadcasting, the producing reservation station is marked not busy. The CDB is a single broadcast channel in the classic design, which means only one result can be sent per cycle; if two units finish in the same cycle, one must wait, creating a structural hazard. Designers mitigate this by adding additional result buses or pipelining writes, trading area for fewer write conflicts. A common misunderstanding is thinking the register file receives results directly from functional units; instead, tag matching at write time determines whether the register accepts a broadcast. The CDB thus implements dynamic forwarding and resolves operand dependencies at write time rather than at commit time.

Let's step through the provided instruction sequence and follow tags and broadcasts across cycles. Begin with registers R1.. R5 valid and all Qi = 0. Cycle 1 issues MUL R6, R2, R4 into RS4 and sets Qi[R6] = RS4. Cycle 2 issues SUB R8, R6, R5 into RS1; because R6 is pending, RS1 records Qj = RS4 while Qk = 0 and sets Qi[R8] = RS1. Also in cycle 2 MUL can start executing because its operands were available. Cycle 3 issues ADD R10, R8, R6 into RS2; RS2 records Qj = RS1 and Qk = RS4 and sets Qi[R10] = RS2. Assume MUL has 3-cycle latency: it completes in cycle 3 and broadcasts its result (6) on the CDB. RS1 captures R6 = 6 and clears Qj. RS2 captures the R6 value for its Qk. Cycle 4 issues DIV into RS5 and ADD into RS3. SUB then begins execution because its operands are ready; when SUB completes in cycle 5 it broadcasts, allowing RS2 to see R8 and start execution. Continue this trace to observe when Qi values return to zero and when registers become valid. The cycle-by-cycle mapping shows where parallelism helped and where dependencies serialized the flow.

Keep these quick reference points handy when you build or debug a Tomasulo simulator. First: when issuing, copy Values only if Qi is zero; otherwise record the producer's tag in Qj/Qk. Second: when a unit completes, broadcast once on the CDB and let all stations and registers attempt tag matching in the same cycle. Third: overwriting Qi assigns future register reads to the newest producer; earlier producers can still broadcast but will not update the register if Qi no longer matches.
